Yeah I was taking a look too. I _think_ the initial title is taken from the console itself as it starts up. And the way Terminal initialises the consoles means that it’s just the exe path by default. 

You can see how it’s hooked up by changing the title from within the console itself - the events hooked up capture this change from within the console itself and updates the tab element in the UI. 

I think we’d need to be careful changing it so that a title change within the console itself continues to allow direct changes from the console. 

Unfortunately I’ve still not figured out a way to set the initial value while preserving the events either. It may just need a manual action as part of the tab creation process, but that would hide something a user puts into their powershell profile script.

@timheuer -- it's likely sync'ing with VT sequence OSC 0/1/2 (all are treated equivalently in the terminal although strictly they shouldn't be). Fire up a pwsh instance and try ```"`e]0;new title`a"``` and you'll see the tab header changes as well as the root window's. The reason it's getting overridden every time is that with every repaint of the buffer, it's emitting the OSC sequence to reset the title. So, in order to change the tab header, you'll need to change state in the VT engine itself; ergo you'll need to emit the right code, at the right time. This may or may not be trivial to do. I'm not that familiar with the codebase.
I'm guessing whenever @miniksa gets proper region invalidation working, the title won't be emitted every frame. Right now the entire buffer is repainted with every keystroke.

I was just having a conversation about this today.

Ideally, the title of tabs will be configurable by the user, either with the path, shell name, name of their pet, etc. all configurable within the profiles.json file.

Additionally, the status bar shown in the video adds another option of where you could display the path if that's something important to you. This feature hasn't been designed yet, so that'll be a little ways out.

See, I'm thinking it should be either 2 or three states:
1. Use title from terminal (this is what we have today)
2. Use a custom string. This could default to the profile name (if we had settings UI), or the user could customize it to whatever.
3. Use profile name. This one feels like a special case of 2.


If we went with just 2 modes, we could do it in the two possible ways:
1. Add an optional `titleText:string` string to the profile. If that's set, then we'll display that string instead of the terminal's title. 
  - this has the downside of not defaulting to the profile name. The user would manually need to set that string.
  - if the profile name changes, then the user would have to manually change this as well.
  - it might not be abundantly clear that `titleText` means we'll be using that instead of the terminal's title, but ideally the settings UI will explain this better, and the actual key doesn't matter so much.
2. Add a `useTerminalTitle:bool` and optional `titleText:string` to the profile. If `useTerminalTitle` is set, then we'll use `titleText`, if it's set. If `titleText` isn't set, then we'll default to the profile name.
  - this has the upside of defaulting to the profile name. 
  - this has the downside of having two settings the user needs to maintain, as opposed to one.
  - could people be confused that having `titleText` set to something, but `useTerminalTitle:false` does _nothing_?

Thoughts? 

<hr>
PS:

Okay, let me break this down.

1. Some users want the title in the tab to match _the title set by the application_
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708046-d54b4280-91b8-11e9-8cb6-3cffbfe40a7e.png)
2. Some users want the title in the tab to match _the title of the profile_
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708076-e4ca8b80-91b8-11e9-87a9-157905b74f8c.png)
3. Some users want the title to be specified separately from the profile _or_ the application.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708111-f6139800-91b8-11e9-9ac0-f4ed050ea1c8.png)

The question is not "how do we store the profile name." (re @mdtauk)

The question is:

If we are designing a robust system that allows a user to specify _one of three options_ (`use app title`, `use profile title`, `use *THIS* title`), **what is most reasonable?**

### A
The easiest way to support all of them is to introduce a nullable _string_ setting, `title`. The downside to `title` is that the user must repeat themselves if they want number 2. Here's what it looks like.

1. `"name": "CMD", "title": null`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708046-d54b4280-91b8-11e9-8cb6-3cffbfe40a7e.png)
1. `"name": "CMD", "title": "CMD"`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708076-e4ca8b80-91b8-11e9-87a9-157905b74f8c.png)
1. `"name": "CMD", "title": "Whatever, I don't care"`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708111-f6139800-91b8-11e9-9ac0-f4ed050ea1c8.png)

### B
The slightly more annoying way to support all of them is to introduce _two settings_, _boolean_ `useAppTitle` and _string_ `title`. This requires two settings. It's more annoying. It also introduces a fourth state that doesn't matter.

1. `"name": "CMD", "useAppTitle": true`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708046-d54b4280-91b8-11e9-8cb6-3cffbfe40a7e.png)
1. `"name": "CMD", "useAppTitle": false, "title": null`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708076-e4ca8b80-91b8-11e9-87a9-157905b74f8c.png)
1. `"name": "CMD", "useAppTitle": false, "title": "Whatever, I don't care"`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708111-f6139800-91b8-11e9-9ac0-f4ed050ea1c8.png)
1. (bonus) `"name": "CMD", "useAppTitle": true, "title": "This is ignored"`
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/14316954/59708046-d54b4280-91b8-11e9-8cb6-3cffbfe40a7e.png)

@DHowett-MSFT  Would providing just a simple CheckBox saying:
> [X] Use profile name in tabs
And then requiring a Name for each Profile, solve this issue?

If the option is unchecked, it displays the system provided text?

Since the settings UI is not looming on the horizon, and its implementation hasn't even started, I am forced to care about _what that checkbox does to the settings file_ :smile:

Also, that still doesn't allow for case 3.

Also, just in general: the settings file is the property of the user, and we have to be good stewards of it. Even if we have a nice fancy settings UI, there will be people who want to edit `profiles.json` themselves in their own text editors and their own tools. We can't just use it as a dumping ground for poorly-thought-out blobs of json. We _have_ to consider the schema when we're designing settings, even if we're approaching it UI first.

> Since the settings UI is not looming on the horizon, and its implementation hasn't even started, I am forced to care about _what that checkbox does to the settings file_ 😄
> 
> Also, that still doesn't allow for case 3.

Sure case 3 is not covered - but do all three scenarios need to be supported?  And of course, you could enforce the JSON to make Profile Names a requirement for a valid profiles.json file.  The CheckBox for overriding the tab text could also be added as a boolean

I think there’s an additional case to consider: runtime modification of the title. I may want my initial title to be “powershell” by default, but to have the ability to change it within the tab itself whilst performing a specific action.

It’s possible that you could handle this by forcing the tab title before handing it over to the users control, and simply allowing modifications like we do at the moment. However I think some applications (e.g. telnet maybe?) which change the window title when executed - that could be contrary to what a user wishes, but supporting the ability might have to just accept this as a side-effect.

I’m not necessarily averse to the decision that we simply don’t allow this to happen when title is specified, but I think we need to explicitly call it out as a decision point.

I think this falls into the string interpolation flexibility, which is planned for post v1.0.  Because of this, I would prefer implementing plan A given above.  If we want to implement any more complexity than that, then we should take the time to design what the end goal looks like for string interpolation and runtime title modification then decide which portion of that goal we want to implement now.  I don't want to see us implement something now that winds up making the end goal harder to achieve.
Is there another issue open for discussing the post-v1 plan?

In the PowerShell world, my `PowerLine` prompt module sets the title automatically, and allows you to override the title with calculated values (don't use this one, it's really long, and is an example only):

I won't fight against the including of a settable `"forceTitleTo" : "Text"` type of property -- but it needs to be a separate property that's _not_ set by default. It should definitely not just default to using the profile name. And frankly, _every time someone asks for the feature_ we should tell them they can set it with `ESC ] 2 ; <title>` in their profile, before we tell them about the feature to override it.

What about WSL? 🤔

> What about WSL? 🤔

More tricky but also way more flexible.  bash in many distributions (re)sets the window title at every prompt via escape codes on PS1.  For example, WSL Ubuntu 18.04 ships with this default in your user's .bashrc:
```shell
case "$TERM" in
  xterm*|rxvt*)
    PS1="\[\e]0;${debian_chroot:+($debian_chroot)}\u@\h: \w\a\]$PS1"
    ;;
  *)
    ;;
esac
```

Pay attention to what appears between `\e]0` (literal "ESC"+"]"+"0") and `\a` (bell or alarm).  
Changing this to:
```shell
 PS1="\[\e]0;ubuntu\a\]$PS1"
```
..yields something that suits my needs:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16697069/60307348-12ba7900-98f9-11e9-9a80-cc3322f1dfbf.png)

_EDIT with a more considered approach_: if you're aiming for a static value, rather than setting the title to the same value at every prompt, just set it once at shell init.  Comment out the entire case\esac sequence that adds the ESC]0 sequence to PS1 in the 1st place, and just add a line to .bashrc to output the same sequence one time:
```shell
echo -e -n "\e]0;ubuntu\a"
```
